items.title: Kevin Parker’s Tame Impala Wins ARIA’s 2026 Global Impact Award
items.summary:
Kevin Parker won’t go home empty handed from the 2026 ARIA Awards.

The Western Australian singer, songwriter, multi-instrumentalist and Tame Impala spearhead will receive the second annual ARIA Global Impact Award, announced ahead of the 40 th annual ARIAs this Wednesday, Nov. 18.

Presented by Spotify, the accolade recognizes Australian recording artists who’ve demonstrated outstanding breakthrough international success and cultural influence, and made an impact for Australian music “through artistry, innovation and global connection” over the previous 12 months.

“I just found out I am this year’s recipient of the Global Impact Award at the ARIAs, which is huge, it’s such an honor, obviously,” enthuses Parker, whose career collection of ARIAs now lifts to 14. “I’m going to be at the ARIA Awards to receive it in person, so I’ll see you there. Thank you.”

Parker has “spent nearly 20 years making records that the rest of the world can’t stop playing. Rihanna has covered him, Lady Gaga and Dua Lipa have brought him into the studio and this year Dracula sank its teeth into the ARIA Top 10 for 18 weeks,” remarks ARIA CEO Annabelle Herd. “He’s shown a generation of Australian artists that a song made in a home studio in Perth can find its biggest audiences in America, Britain, Mexico and Brazil. Congratulations Kevin from all of us at ARIA.”

Dom Dolla was the inaugural recipient of the award , which is presented at the discretion of the ARIA board to an artist whose international efforts are said to exemplify Australia’s influence in contemporary music worldwide.

Parker…
items.t: Kevin Parker’s Tame Impala Wins ARIA’s 2026 Global Impact Award

items.title: U.K. Labels Veteran Ferdy Unger-Hamilton Joins Gotobeat Advisory Board
items.summary:
Ex-Columbia Records U.K. president Ferdy Unger-Hamilton joins the advisory board of Gotobeat, a business that describes its mission as “building a new model for live entertainment.”

With Unger-Hamilton on board, enthuses Max Busin , CEO and founder of Gotobeat, the company enjoys a “significant step” forward. “What a moment this is for Gotobeat,” he remarks. “We’re building a company that combines the experience and relationships that have always driven the music industry with technology that allows us to operate in a completely different way. Ferdy understands that vision, and I’m really looking forward to building the next chapter of Gotobeat with him.”

A decade ago, in 2016 , Unger-Hamilton was promoted to lead Columbia Records’ U.K., following senior leadership roles at Virgin and Polydor Records, where he helped launch Ellie Goulding, The 1975, Lana Del Rey, Haim, Years & Years and Michael Kiwanuka.

Earlier, in 2014, he founded Promised Land Music, where he helped launch the career of Fred again…

Based in London, Gotobeat presents itself as a “next-generation” live music promoter and ticketing platform that uses proprietary data and artificial intelligence to design, price, and launch tours and festivals across the United Kingdom and Europe.

Unger-Hamilton takes his seat as the company prepares for its next phase of growth in markets, including projects focused on Latin music events.

“What excites me about Gotobeat is that it understands both sides of the music industry: the importance of relationships, instinct and experience, and the opportunity to use data…
items.t: U.K. Labels Veteran Ferdy Unger-Hamilton Joins Gotobeat Advisory Board

items.title: Live Nation’s 17,000 Gather Brisbane Project Is Approved
items.summary:
BRISBANE, Australia – The capital of the Sunshine State, Brisbane, will become a two-arena city when a new 17,000-capacity venue is completed ahead of the 2032 Summer Olympic and Paralympic Games.

A years-long wait for approval came to end this week when Gather Brisbane was rubber stamped, a major new live music and entertainment project for the inner-city suburb of Woolloongabba.

Live Nation, OVG and Plenary will build the arena, which will have an 18,700 capacity in concert mode and which, the team behind it say, should bring more major live events to Brisbane.

According to forecasts presented by Live Nation, the arena is expected to welcome more than 1.2 million people each year, support upwards of 1,500 ongoing jobs and generate almost A$844 million ($568 million) annually for the city’s visitor economy.

“Brisbane has the audience and the ambition to welcome more of the world’s biggest tours, but it needs the venues to match,” comments Michael Coppel, chairman of Live Nation Australia and New Zealand. “This arena will help bring more shows to Queensland, strengthen Australia’s appeal as a touring destination and give artists and fans an arena they can be proud of for decades to come.”

Brisbane won the rights to host the Olympics in 2021 when the IOC declared the city as the “preferred candidate,” thanks to its proven track record for organizing international events, with the Commonwealth Games (two, including the Gold Coast), an Expo and the Goodwill Games in its good books.

And critically, the region already had  up to 90% of the essential pieces of…
items.t: Live Nation’s 17,000 Gather Brisbane Project Is Approved

items.title: Noah Kahan Reacts to 2027 Grammy Nominations Snub: ‘I Was In My Feelings for a Sec’
items.summary:
Before the 2027 Grammy nominations were announced on Monday morning, Noah Kahan was expected to have a big presence across the Big Four categories with his latest album The Great Divide . But once all the nominees were revealed, Kahan only had a single nomination: best contemporary folk album.

The singer/songwriter became the poster child for countless “snubs & surprises” lists ( Billboard ‘s included ), and the only thing fans heard from Kahan on Monday was this three-word tweet: “Life goes on.”

But he had more to say on Tuesday (Nov. 17), taking to X to thank fans and congratulate his fellow nominees.

“Needed a day to just recalibrate but I want to say THANK YOU so much for the support and love,” he wrote. “I also want to offer a huge congratulations to every nominee. They all deserve it and I am proud to have been considered in the same company!”

He ended the message on this upbeat note: “Onward.”

items.title: DistroKid Gives AI Upload Data to UMG and Sony for Suno Copyright Lawsuit After Initial Refusal
items.summary:
Amid legal pressure from Universal Music Group (UMG) and Sony Music, DistroKid has provided data about the prevalence of AI-generated music moving through its pipes.

A Monday (Nov. 16) court filing, obtained by Billboard , says DistroKid has complied with the third-party subpoena served by UMG and Sony as part of their copyright infringement lawsuit against AI music service Suno. The subpoena sought numbers regarding how much of the music that passes through the leading DIY digital distributor is thought to be made with Suno and other AI generators.

Related 

‘AI-Generated Slop’: UMG Sues DistroKid for ‘Flooding’ Streaming Platforms With Junk Music 

CL Signs With THEBLACKLABEL, Reuniting With Longtime Producer Teddy For 'Full Circle' Moment 

Severe Weather, Radius Clauses and Finding the Next Generation of Festival Headliners: 'It's a Year-by-Year Fight to Stay Alive' 

UMG and Sony say this data is key to proving that Suno-generated music is eating into their market share and royalty distributions. Competition between AI songs and human music is a key part of the “fair use” inquiry — that is, the test a judge will use to decide the seismic question of whether Suno infringed the majors’ copyrights by training on millions of unlicensed tracks. DistroKid is not a party to the Suno suit.

DistroKid initially refused to provide AI data to UMG and Sony, leading the labels to initiate a legal action last month seeking to force compliance with the subpoena. The distributor has since changed its tune and produced responsive documents, according to Monday’s court filing, which…
items.t: DistroKid Gives AI Upload Data to UMG and Sony for Suno Copyright Lawsuit After Initial Refusal

items.title: Cody Johnson on Why He’s Skipping 2026 CMA Awards: ‘Going 100 MPH All the Time Isn’t Healthy’
items.summary:
Cody Johnson has four nominations heading into the 2026 CMA Awards and was set to perform at the show, but the country star revealed Tuesday (Nov. 17) that he won’t be attending the ceremony after all.

In a note posted to Instagram , Johnson addressed his “CoJo Nation” fans, his peers and the country music industry at large to let them know why he wouldn’t be at Wednesday night’s show.

Related

Here Are the Performers & Presenters for the 2026 CMA Awards

“I won’t be attending the CMA Awards tomorrow, and I want to be honest about why,” Johnson wrote. “After getting sick at the end of my UK tour earlier this month, I realized much of it stemmed from mental and physical exhaustion. I want to be open about this because I believe we help one another by revealing our truths, and this time my truth isn’t in the words of a song; it’s real life.

“At the end of the day, I’m a human being, no matter how much I tell myself and others I’m Superman,” he continued. “I have everything to be thankful for, but sometimes I put too much pressure on myself. I’m going to spend some time recouping at home; being grounded by my family is what I need most right now.”

Johnson is nominated for five awards at Wednesday night’s show, including the top prize of entertainer of the year. In his note, he acknowledged just how hard he’s worked to reach that upper echelon of country music.

items.title: Travis Scott and Don Toliver Sued Over Sample on Hit JACKBOYS Track ‘What To Do?’
items.summary:
Travis Scott , Don Toliver and other collaborators in the hip-hop collective JACKBOYS are facing a copyright lawsuit over their 2019 track “What To Do?”.

The JACKBOYS team was sued on Tuesday (Nov. 17) by Niv Kalisky, an Israeli music producer who goes by “Early Yellow.” The lawsuit, obtained and first reported by Billboard , alleges that Kalisky hasn’t gotten the master points he deserves for creating a sample used by the Scott-led collective of artists from his label, Cactus Jack Records.

Related 

Travis Scott No Longer Facing Lawsuit Over ‘Alright’ Sample on ‘Astroworld’ and ‘Utopia’ 

CL Signs With THEBLACKLABEL, Reuniting With Longtime Producer Teddy For 'Full Circle' Moment 

Severe Weather, Radius Clauses and Finding the Next Generation of Festival Headliners: 'It's a Year-by-Year Fight to Stay Alive' 

“What To Do?” was one of seven tracks on the group’s self-titled 2019 album JACKBOYS , which debuted at No. 1 on the Billboard 200 and was followed up last summer by another chart-topping set , JACKBOYS 2 . The song itself charted at No. 56 on the Billboard Hot 100 and No. 20 on Billboard ‘s Hot Rap Songs chart.

Kalisky is credited as a songwriter and additional producer on “What To Do?”, meaning he has received publishing income for the composition. But the lawsuit claims he’s also entitled to master royalties for providing the track’s producers with a sample beat that was later mixed into the final sound recording. 

According to the complaint, Kalisky’s lawyers sent multiple royalty requests over the years to both Cactus Jack and its distribution partner,…
items.t: Travis Scott and Don Toliver Sued Over Sample on Hit JACKBOYS Track ‘What To Do?’

items.summary:
Interpol have announced their biggest US headline show to date, featuring support from IDLES , Wisp and more.

The milestone gig will be held at the Los Angeles BMO Stadium on Friday May 24, 2027. With a capacity of up to 24,000 people, it will surpass the band’s previous largest US headline performance, which was held at the State Historic Park in LA back in 2017.

Frontman Paul Banks and co. will be joined by a IDLES, as well as Molchat Doma and Wisp on the night, and the announcement comes as NYC indie icons are currently on the road with Bloc Party across the UK and Europe , celebrating the release of their acclaimed eighth studio album, ‘ This Mirror Weighs a Ton ’.

Tickets for the Los Angeles go on sale on Friday (November 20) at 10am PT, and pre-sales begin on Thursday (November 19) at the same time. Visit here for tickets and more information.

View this post on Instagram 

The gig in Los Angeles next May will be mark Interpol’s biggest US headline show to date. The biggest gig they have ever played took place in 2024, when the band drew over 200,000 people to Mexico City’s Zócalo .

The announcement of the show comes as Interpol got their first ever Grammy nomination yesterday (Monday November 16) – shortlisted in the Best Album Cover category alongside Lily Allen , Mavis Staples , Rapsody and 21 Savage .

Last week, the band kicked off their huge co-headline tour with Bloc Party with an opening night in Berlin – having previously toured the UK…

items.summary:
Muse played the second of their two shows at The O2 last night (Monday November 16) and broke out the live debut of Ellie Goulding collab ‘Hush’. Check it out below.

READ MORE: Matt Bellamy on rediscovering his own muse: “I can’t live without music – that feeling came back to me on this album” 

The gig was the latest of the Devonshire trio’s ‘ The Wow! Signal ’ UK tour dates, following things kicking off in Manchester last week with an ambitious new stage production, before heading to the capital on Sunday (November 15).

Dates come in support of their acclaimed 10th album , which dropped back in June, and follow on from a run of North American shows earlier this year.

While night two at The O2 largely followed the same setlist as the night prior – kicking things off with new tracks ‘Hexagon’ and ‘The Sickness In You & I’, before going into fan favourites including ‘Knights Of Cydonia’, ‘Hysteria’, ‘Supermassive Black Hole’ and ‘Uprising’, the second show saw them introduce their Ellie Goulding collaboration ‘Hush’ for the first time.

For the majority of the song, frontman Matt Bellamy performed from the hexagonal b-stage, while bandmates Chris Wolstenholme and Dominic Howard stayed on the main stage, backed by an immersive light display.

While Goulding didn’t make a guest appearance on the night, she did appear on the screens, singing along to the song while looking straight into the camera, as Bellamy duetted with her playback vocals.

items.title: Coldplay’s Chris Martin and Jonny Buckland announce intimate London Christmas 2026 charity show
items.summary:
Chris Martin and Jonny Buckland of Coldplay have announced another one of their intimate London Christmas shows for 2026, with proceeds going to charity.

READ MORE: Coldplay interview: “When things appear overwhelmingly positive, that’s often because it’s what the singer needs most” 

The gig will see the singer and the guitarist return to the usual site of Hackney Church on Tuesday December 15, and perform a special, intimate show to raise funds for Crisis and Choose Love .

They have made it into a tradition to play festive, one-off shows in London around Christmas – having first headed to the venue for a gig in 2011 , and following it up with another gig in 2015. 

In 2024, Martin and Buckland went on to play another special gig at the venue and raised over £350,000 for homeless charity Crisis in just two days along the way, and last year they headed back for another festive show – donating proceeds to both Crisis and War Child.

Now, they have confirmed a 2026 gig, which will mark the pair’s only public concert of 2026. As seen over the past two years, proceeds will be donated to Crisis to help support those facing homelessness, and proceeds this year will also be donated to Choose Love – offering emergency aid and life-changing support to refugees and displaced people around the world.

Chris Martin and Jonny Buckland Christmas 2026 show poster 
 At the shows, both Martin and Buckland perform stripped back versions of their Coldplay tracks, and are usually joined by classical musicians and a few surprise guests.

Tickets are available now via a prize draw – which is…
items.t: Coldplay’s Chris Martin and Jonny Buckland announce intimate London Christmas 2026 charity show

items.title: Julien Baker announces new album ‘This World Or The Next’ with epic single ‘Hound’
items.summary:
Julien Baker has announced new album ‘This World Or The Next’ and dropped the explosive lead single ‘Hound’.

READ MORE: Julien Baker & Torres – ‘Send A Prayer My Way’ review: a hearty embrace of country’s tried-and-tested conventions 

Set for release on February 12, 2027, via Matador, it is the fourth solo album from Baker – following on from 2015’s ‘Sprained Ankle’, 2017’s ‘Turn Out the Lights’ and 2021’s ‘ Little Oblivions ’. It also marks their first new music since dropping ‘ The Record ’ with Boygenius in 2023 and the collaborative album with Torres, ‘Send a Prayer My Way’ , last year. Pre-order it here .

With ‘This World Or The Next’, Baker reunited with longtime friends and collaborators Matt Gilliam and Calvin Lauber, and embraced more explosive guitar riffs and intimate lyricism than ever before.

To accompany the album announcement, Baker has dropped the lead single ‘Hound’ – an epic, experimental track that explores how ego can get in the way of love. It starts with a hypnotic glitching piano, before exploding into intense guitar riffs, anthemic melodies, and heartfelt, cathartic vocals.

The reunion between Baker and Gilliam comes as they played together in their early band, Forrister, for years before Baker dropped debut solo album ‘Sprained Ankle’ in 2015. For Lauber, the producer has worked with Baker on ‘Turn Out The Lights’ and ‘Little Oblivions’, and also appeared on stage as their touring guitarist.

Across the album, the trio recapture that feeling of what it was like to first start working with one another, and each anticipating what the future…

items.title: They’re one of the UK’s greatest cult bands – who swore they’d never reunite. What brought Life Without Buildings back together?
items.summary:
The Scottish quartet existed for just three years at the turn of the millennium. But after Frank Ocean and TikTok thrilled to Sue Tompkins’ unique vocals, they’re back. They explain their fears about ‘spoiling the joy’

‘I’m excited, I’m scared, I’m anxious – that bubbling feeling, like when you’re on a rollercoaster, at the very top, just before the big drop.”

On a drizzly afternoon in July, huddled with her three bandmates in the cramped cupboard that’s the dressing room of Glasgow venue Mono, Sue Tompkins is managing her feelings ahead of her first proper gig with Life Without Buildings in almost a quarter of a century. “Everybody coming is invited, it’s secret, nobody paid much to get in, the profits are going to charity,” adds guitarist Robert Dallas Gray, sat beside her, as much to steady his own nerves as to explain the circumstances of tonight’s show. “I hope people aren’t looking at it like we’re fucking entertainers.”

items.title: ‘Mick Jagger should fold up his penis and go home’: the caustic genius of music critic Robert Christgau
items.summary:
Beloved for his savage takedowns and rhapsodic raves, the legendary Village Voice reviewer opens up in a candid new documentary

Rows and rows of CDs, albums, cassettes and books creak and groan on shelves that snake around the walls and choke the halls of an apartment in New York City’s East Village. The clutter that sprawls through its rooms is so dense it suggests the twistiest parts of a Moroccan medina or a warren no self-respecting rabbit would allow. Buried amid the muddle is a man hunched over a computer keyboard, clacking out words meant to make sense of all the sounds that these physical media hold.

Welcome to the lair of Robert Christgau, the self-declared “Dean of American Rock Critics”, as seen in a new documentary provocatively titled The Last Critic. “Bob is someone who has probably listened to more music, and published more words about music, than anyone to walk the face of the earth, and he’s still doing it in his mid-80s,” says Matty Wishnow, who directed the film. “It’s a career that’s both unprecedented and unrepeatable.”

Continue reading...
items.t: ‘Mick Jagger should fold up his penis and go home’: the caustic genius of music critic Robert Christgau

items.title: ‘I have to sell my bum on OnlyFans to go on tour’: Kate Nash on fame, feminism and fighting the music business
items.summary:
She threw a (metaphorical) brick through Spotify’s window and exposed industry failings with her ‘Butts for Tour Buses’ campaign. Now the singer is embracing her Irish roots with her new album’s fighting spirit

Kate Nash was standing on a fire truck in a showgirl outfit complete with white tights and pink G-string, shouting through a loudhailer about the music industry’s failure to pay artists fairly, when she wondered if she’d gone too far. It was 2024 and the truck, which made pit stops outside the London offices of Spotify and Live Nation, had a large black-and-white picture of Nash’s bum on the back along with the words “Butts for Tour Buses” – a reference to her newly launched OnlyFans account, which she was using to fund her tour.

That afternoon, she called her manager Kat. “I told her: ‘I’ve thrown a brick through the window at Spotify.’ She went: ‘What, literally?’ and I said: ‘No, but I’ve been standing outside their offices with a megaphone, so that relationship is over. I don’t think we’ll be making their New Music Friday feature.’ And we didn’t.” [see footnote]

items.t: ‘I have to sell my bum on OnlyFans to go on tour’: Kate Nash on fame, feminism and fighting the music business

items.title: Ocean Colour Scene review – no other band of their era can do it like this
items.summary:
Ulster Hall, Belfast
With two sets of fathers and sons now in the group, as they play all of Moseley Shoals on its 30th anniversary, the indie stalwarts have aged into seismic and soulful performers

‘It’s only 30 years ago,” Simon Fowler says of Moseley Shoals. He would seem to mean it, but 30 years makes Ocean Colour Scene’s breakthrough album as old now as Revolver was when they were making it. The band once derided for raiding the 60s are now heritage themselves. They open the album’s anniversary tour on the stage where Led Zeppelin first played Stairway to Heaven, and you can’t help but appreciate the lineage.

They walk on to Green Onions, fresh from the Crown Bar, and open with You’ve Got It Bad, all supreme Motown stomp. Fowler sings with a hand in his pocket and looks taken aback by the welcome. The casualness is a conduit: his voice has aged into something close to peak Joe Cocker, grained at the edges, honey underneath. Lining Your Pockets is more resounding than ever.

Continue reading...
items.t: Ocean Colour Scene review – no other band of their era can do it like this

items.title: Paris Paloma review – arena-scale alt-pop drama from a singer on her way to bigger things
items.summary:
Bristol Beacon
The UK artist combines feminist fury with accessible melodies and a dramatic flair that sees her alternately pogoing and seeking out the wind machines at the prow of the stage

People are dancing to a song they don’t know, with flower garlands in their hair and their arms around their friends. This reaction to Fairy Dance, an unreleased track written about the community that has sprung up around her music, says a lot about the moment Paris Paloma finds herself in, and tonight’s show feels for all the world like a stepping stone to bigger things.

Throughout, Paloma leans in to the built-in drama of songs from her second album, The Fatal Flaw, which pairs ornate folk arrangements with the sort of arena-sized alt-pop production favoured by Florence + the Machine. With a sculpture inspired by surrealist Ithell Colquhoun’s Tree of Veins dominating the stage, she falls to her knees to deliver high notes and seeks out wind machines at the prow of the stage, her flowing crimson dress buffeted as if on a wintry moor.

items.t: Paris Paloma review – arena-scale alt-pop drama from a singer on her way to bigger things

items.title: James Blunt: ‘Do I have a nickname? Yes, it rhymes with blunt’
items.summary:
The singer on his love for Ibiza, the weirdest thing he’s done in the name of romance, and being signed up for Celebrity Traitors against his will

You were a punching bag for such a long time after You’re Beautiful became a massive hit but your consistent good humour is deeply admirable. Does it ever get tiring?

It was a surprise, at the beginning. I was just a little guy with a dream. And when you achieve your dream, you think people would be happy for you. For them not to be happy for you but angry with you, for your song, seems irrational, an overreaction. It is interesting how people generally want to tear people down for achieving their little dreams. But I’d had a real proper job before that [as a captain in the British army]. My friends might have been on operations in Afghanistan or Iraq, so if I were to complain to them at the time saying, “Oh, the Guardian said something really horrid about me and gave me three stars for my album” – they would be able to talk about who had lost their lives or limbs that day, and that put it all in perspective. And perspective is everything.

Continue reading...
items.t: James Blunt: ‘Do I have a nickname? Yes, it rhymes with blunt’

items.title: Sheherazaad: Khudgarzi review | Ammar Kalia's global album of the month
items.summary:
(Erased Tapes)
Dreamy, reverb-laden arrangements, virtuosic vocals and echoes of PJ Harvey and Massive Attack make this disarming debut a one-of-a-kind creation

Since the release of her debut EP, Qasr, in 2024, south Asian-American vocalist and composer Sheherazaad has developed a distinctive take on the classical singing of her heritage. While her contemporaries such as the singers Ganavya and Manizeh draw on spiritual vocal traditions, and Arooj Aftab on jazz and folk instrumentation, Sheherazaad’s work is darker and far more introspective, using sparse acoustic arrangements to create a style of Urdu-language noir.

On this debut album, she delivers her most disarmingly eerie and mournful work yet. A heavy layer of reverb coats the record’s spare and often evocative arrangements, making undulating tabla hits echo beneath Sheherazaad’s keening vocals on Qatil, while on Registaan it lends an unnervingly distorted quality to a simple guitar refrain and on Mard it subsumes melody in a haze of resonance. The resulting atmosphere sits somewhere between PJ Harvey’s late-90s eerie grunge and the trip-hop qawwali of Massive Attack’s work with singer Nusrat Fateh Ali Khan – an ambience that is…
items.t: Sheherazaad: Khudgarzi review | Ammar Kalia's global album of the month

items.title: ‘Would you breastfeed your own father?’ The goofy, spiky world of art-pop duo Charlotte Adigéry and Bolis Pupul
items.summary:
After wittily blending pop and politics on their debut, the Belgians are now processing their personal lives. We join them for a mindbending tour of their home city of Ghent

Boris Kor Tom Zeebroek is staring up at a grey gothic building in the centre of Ghent, squinting through the late September sun that is covering his home town in a cloak of unseasonal warmth.

Zeebroek is encouraging his bandmate Charlotte Adigéry and I to crane our necks towards the Mammelokker, an 18th-century Flemish relief on the top of the building. It’s a gruesome bit of stone, which sits above the town square and depicts a daughter suckling her own father. The pair are taking me on a tour of their medieval home town, and this disturbing architectural decoration is part of our itinerary.

items.title: Snoh Aalegra: Legendary Love review – raw R&B talent restrained by reverence for the greats
items.summary:
(Stem)
Her truly remarkable, Sade-ish voice is hypnotic against some dizzyingly plush production, but a modern spin on 80s pastiche sometimes veers too close to tribute

Swedish-Iranian singer Snoh Aalegra has previously described her music – a lush, pastiche-y mix of R&B, hip-hop, soul and pop – as “cinematic soul”. But although she’s a dab hand at graceful, timeless presentation (and has a truly remarkable voice) Aalegra’s music has often struggled to match up to its aesthetic, hampered by her love of the greats and a penchant for broadly generic lyrics. Her most recent album, 2021’s Temporary Highs in the Violet Skies, made some headway toward carving out a more distinctive sound, thanks to sparky and inventive production from Tyler, the Creator, No ID, P2J and the Neptunes, but still didn’t quite feel like the right fit.

Aalegra’s fourth album is her most successful front-to-back statement yet, even if she can’t shake off the talent-show-ish reverence for her idols. Sparse and warm, Legendary Love puts her androgynous, Sade-ish voice in dizzyingly plush environments: a hybrid of Afrobeats and 80s R&B on the hypnotic I Love You; a bed of minimalist guitars and moonlit synths on This That, which sounds as though it could have been produced by Jai Paul.
items.t: Snoh Aalegra: Legendary Love review – raw R&B talent restrained by reverence for the greats
